metadata.title: Buckley v. American Constitutional Law Foundation, Inc., 525 U.S. 182 (1999) (No. 97-930)
metadata.description:
Case name: Buckley v. American Constitutional Law Foundation, Inc.

Opinion filed: 1999-01-12

Docket No.: 97-930

Citations:
• 142 L. Ed. 2d 599
• 119 S. Ct. 636
• 525 U.S. 182
• 1999 U.S. LEXIS 506

Case holding summaries:
• state requirement forcing petitioners to wear identification badge violated First Amendment because it infringed on petitioners' anonymity
• holding that the First Amendment was violated by a Colorado statute that required persons who circulated petitions for an initiative to wear identification badges revealing their names
• invalidating, on First Amendment Grounds, a Colorado statute that required initiative petition circulators to wear identification badges
• noting the risk of quid pro quo corruption "when money is paid to, or for, candidates"
• invalidating statute requiring initiative petitioners to wear identification badges as violation First Amendment
• "But the First Amendment requires us to be vigilant . . . to guard against undue hindrances to political conversations and the exchange of ideas."
• “’exact- ing scrutiny’ is necessary when compelled disclosure of cam- paign-related payments is at issue”
• "The Court of Appeals did not rule on the constitutionality of other elements of the badge provision, namely the `requirement that the badge disclose whether the circulator is paid of a volunteer, and if paid, by whom.' Nor do we." (citations omitted)
• concluding that a requirement that petition circulators be registered voters implicated “core political speech” no less than the “fleeting encounter” of leafletting or the more 28 involved “discussion of the merits” that attended the petition circulation
• upholding a registration requirement for paid petition circulators while striking down a "name badge" requirement
• acknowledging that "there must be a substantial regulation of elections if they are to be fair and honest and if some sort of order, rather than chaos, is to accompany the democratic processes"
• state residence requirement "more precisely achieve[s] the State's subpoena service objective" than voter registration requirement (internal quotation marks omitted)
• "The ease with which qualified [individuals] may register to vote . . . does not lift the burden on speech" placed by voter registration requirement for petition circulators
• same for state statute requiring election initiative petition circulators to wear identification badges, but approving statute requiring circulators to file as a public record an identifying affidavit that revealed their names and other personal information
• considering the burden of eliminating from the pool of potential circulators "[a]t least 400,000 persons eligible to vote" who "were not registered"
• involving the circulation of ballot-initiative petitions
• requiring the “[l]isting [of] paid circulators and their income from circulation”
• holding unconstitutional a requirement that initiative petition circulators be registered voters
• “But the First Amendment requires us to be vigilant . . . to guard against undue hindrances to political conversations and the exchange of ideas.”
• "Even a pure message of support, unadorned with reasons, is valuable to the democratic process"
• "Colorado acknowledges there are at least 400,000 qualified but unregistered voters in the state."
• upholding Michigan procedures for checking voters' signatures on initiative petitions
• Kentucky's regulation of candidate campaign promises
• "[T]he First Amendment requires us to be vigilant ... to guard against undue hindrances to political conversations and the exchange of ideas."
• upholding single subject and unambiguous title requirements for initiative proposals to amend Florida's Constitution
• "The risk of corruption perceived in cases involving candidate elections . . . simply is not present in a popular vote on a public issue."
• Massachusetts law prohibiting certain business entities from making expenditures for the purpose of affecting referendum votes
• Tennessee law prohibiting solicitation of voters and distribution of campaign literature within 100 feet of the entrance of a polling place
• "We recognize that a State's enforcement interest might justify a more limited identification requirement, but Ohio has shown scant cause for inhibiting the leafletting at issue here."
• stating, further, that the challenged restriction reduced the chances that initiative proponents would gather signatures sufficient in number to qualify for the ballot, and thus limited proponents' "ability to make the matter the focus of statewide discussion"
• describing disclosure provisions of Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971
• observing that an "informed public opinion is the most potent of all restraints upon misgovernment"
• first determining that California's prohibition on primary endorsements by the official governing bodies of political parties burdened speech and association and then applying strict scrutiny
• holding that time limits on enrollment in political parties did not violate the right of association because individuals were not prohibited from enrolling in parties
• upholding requirement that voters enroll as members of a political party prior to voting in a primary election on the ground that the regulation did not impose an onerous burden and advanced a legitimate state interest
• upholding qualifications to vote in primary
• upholding Minnesota law that banned fusion candidacies on the ground that the State had asserted a "sufficiently weighty" interest
• disclosure of names, addresses, and payments made to the circulators of ballot-initiative petitions forced them to surrender anonymity and was unjustifiable inhibition on free speech
• describing petition circulation as “core political speech”
• overturning various registration requirements for petition circulators
• striking down a Colorado statute requiring initiative-petition circulators be registered voters
• recognizing the state’s “strong interest in policing lawbreakers among peti‐ tion circulators”
• noting that under First Amendment, petition circulation "is core political speech because it involves interactive communication concerning political change" (internal quotations omitted)
• discussing factual record established at bench trial and by cross-motions for summary judgment
• requiring petition circulators to wear identifying badges forces them to reveal their identity at the same time they deliver their political message thus exposing them to "heat of the moment" harassment
• holding unconstitutional a Colorado law requiring that ballot initiative petition circulators be registered voters
• invalidating Colorado's requirement that petition circulators for ballot initiatives be registered voters of the State
• petition circulation is core political speech protected by first amendment
• recognizing “there must be a substantial regulation of elections if they are to be fair and honest”
• recognizing “there must be a substantial regulation of elections . . . if some sort of order, rather than chaos, is to accompany the democratic process”
